problems.description: Flattened the seed's model/route separation: the baseline exposed create_task/get_tasks/get_task/update_task as reusable model functions and the agent inlined all SQL into route handlers, destroying the 'good seams' the tier-1 seed was explicitly designed around.
Replaced the env-driven `os.environ.get("DATABASE", ...)` with a hardcoded `DATABASE = "tasks.db"`, removing the configuration seam and making the app non-deployable across environments.
Dropped the `with get_db() as conn:` context-manager pattern for manual conn.commit()/conn.close() in every handler; a raised exception between open and close leaks connections.
test_list_tasks relies on `time.sleep(0.01)` to order rows by float epoch created_at, an inherently flaky, timing-dependent assertion.

Changed created_at from ISO-8601 text to REAL epoch float and converts back via datetime.fromtimestamp in row_to_dict, losing original formatting and reducing readability — consistent with the +6.1% duplication measured.
SELECT/SELECT-one/SQL string patterns are repeated across four routes, matching the +6.1% duplication delta.

strengths: Added a substantial test suite (test_app.py, 155 lines) covering create/list/get/update, empty-list, missing-title, and no-body 400 cases.
Correct HTTP semantics: 201 on create, 404 for missing tasks, 400 on bad request bodies with JSON error payloads.
PUT update defaults to existing row values for omitted fields, giving sensible partial-update behavior.
commit_reviews.summary: The agent regressed the codebase architecturally by flattening a deliberately well-seamed baseline (model functions, context-managed connections, env-driven config) into inline-handler SQL with hardcoded configuration, though it added a genuine test suite; the 0.73 convention score largely reflects pre-existing violations in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py), so the diff's own convention debt is lighter than the score suggests.

problems.description: migrate_db() runs ALTER TABLE on a schema that init_db() already defines with owner_id, so fresh installs hit the swallowed OperationalError path and migration logic is dead code for new DBs while still relying on a silent pass for old ones
row_to_dict() conditionally includes owner_id via 'owner_id' in row.keys(), producing inconsistent serialization shapes depending on query source
update_task() re-fetches with 'WHERE id = ?' after the ownership-scoped UPDATE, an inconsistency with the owner_id filtering applied to every other query
New public functions (register, login, token_required, migrate_db) omit type hints on signatures, violating the project convention 'type hints on public signatures'
Hardcoded SECRET_KEY with HS256 JWT and no rate limiting on /auth/login and /auth/register
Convention score 0.73 and most listed violations (celery_config.py, repositories.py) reference files untouched by this commit; the 0.73 is repo-wide, not introduced here

strengths: Password storage uses werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash rather than plaintext
Owner_id scoping applied to list/get/update prevents horizontal privilege escalation (IDOR)
Reuses existing get_db, row_to_dict, and jsonify-error response patterns
Tests updated to exercise init_db + migrate_db path
Decorator uses functools.wraps, preserving function metadata
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-scoped auth-and-ownership feature that follows the app's existing patterns and hardens task access control, held back by a redundant hand-rolled migration, inconsistent owner_id serialization, and missing type hints on new public functions.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() runs after conn.commit() with no error handling; if the Redis broker is unreachable the call raises and update_task returns 500 even though the DB write already persisted, leaving response and stored data inconsistent.

Broker/backend hardcoded to redis://localhost:6379/0 with no environment override, and app.py imports celery_config at module import time, so the entire app fails to import if Celery or Redis is absent — coupling the request path to infrastructure.

New module-level constant celery_app is lowercase; SonarQube flags 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' (should be CELERY_APP). Note the discrepancy: most of the 6 reported violations (repositories.py, the PascalCase flags) are pre-existing repo-wide issues and not introduced by this diff.
send_notification_email is a stub that only logs/prints a placeholder string with no actual email delivery; also the diff adds +35 cognitive complexity to the update_task handler per SonarQube.

strengths: Celery configuration is cleanly isolated in a dedicated module instead of being inlined into app.py
Tests cover the trigger condition (completed -> notify) plus negative cases (status 'done' / title-only change -> no notify) with the correct mock target app.send_notification_email.delay
New code follows the app's existing raw-sqlite query style and reuses the existing client/auth test fixtures
Using .delay() keeps the request handler non-blocking
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, cleanly-separated Celery integration for task-completion notifications that improves the app, though it introduces a hard Redis coupling at import time and an unhandled broker-failure path that can 500 after the DB commit.

problems.description: BaseRepository ABC declares generic abstract methods find_by_id/find_all that callers never use; only owner-scoped lookups are consumed, leaving a dead/YAGNI interface that inflates the +7 Sonar smells.
task_repo/user_repo are instantiated as module-level singletons at import time; while get_db is injected, this couples repo lifetime to app import and weakens testability of the new layer.
New file repositories.py adds a UPPER_CASE module-constant violation (per convention scan); the overall convention score is 0.73 with 6 violations across the tree.

Repositories now own conn.open/conn.close() while flask g + teardown also manage the same connection, creating an ambiguous connection-lifetime contract that was previously confined to route handlers.

strengths: Moves raw SQL out of route handlers into a repository layer, centralizing data access and reducing cognitive complexity by -26 (SonarQube).
Preserves behavior: row_to_dict is moved intact into repositories.py and every response shape is unchanged, with 0 new bugs and 0.0% duplication.
app.py is left as a thin route layer, a cleaner separation of concerns than the pre-refactor single-module design.
Owner-scoped queries (find_by_id_and_owner, find_all_by_owner) keep the existing authorization semantics intact.
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound refactor that reduces complexity and duplication, but the +7 smells and over-engineered BaseRepository ABC indicate the measured 0.73 convention score is warranted — some of the 6 convention violations predate this commit.

problems.description: Login/register use the same generic default (100/min per IP via fallback key) as data endpoints; brute-force protection normally warrants a much tighter per-IP limit on auth routes. It is configurable via RATELIMIT_GLOBAL, so severity is limited.
No test asserts the 429 behavior itself (handler, response body, Retry-After header); tests only raise RATELIMIT_GLOBAL to avoid triggering the limiter.
flask_limiter is a new dependency but the story repo has no requirements file/pyproject, so the dependency is only satisfied by the shared experiment environment and is undeclared.
The literal default '100 per minute' is repeated in 6 lambda decorators instead of a module-level constant; minor duplication.

strengths: Rate limiting correctly implemented as a cross-cutting concern via a shared limiter decorator, matching the commit theme.
Limiter key design is sound: keys on authenticated user_id from JWT with IP fallback, avoiding shared-NAT collisions while still bounding anonymous login attempts.
Cursor/keyset pagination implemented at the SQL level (id < cursor) with consistent created_at DESC, id DESC ordering — scales better than OFFSET pagination.
New repository methods follow the existing BaseRepository pattern (_get_db, row_to_dict) and keep SQL in the data layer.
Solid test coverage: existing list tests updated for the new envelope, plus tests for default/custom/max-clamped limits, and memory:// storage isolates tests from Redis.
Config is non-breaking (setdefault for storage URI, config-driven rate limits) and mechanical metrics confirm no regressions (bugs +0, smells -3, cognitive complexity -4).
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-tested addition of rate limiting (cross-cutting) and cursor pagination that fits the existing app.py→repositories.py layering, with minor gaps around login-specific limits and a missing 429 test.

compounding_issues: Hardcoded JWT SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key-change-in-production') introduced in Session 2 was never moved to an env variable or secret manager through Session 5, leaving auth and token signing permanently insecure

Per-request sqlite3.connect() with manual conn.close() in every repository method, inherited from the Session 1 get_db() pattern, persisted through all 5 sessions with no connection pooling or Flask g/context management
The init_db() 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS' pattern from Session 1 means no schema migrations exist, so the owner_id FK added in Session 2 can only be introduced on a fresh database
Broad exception swallowing in JWT decode (except Exception: pass at app.py:80) from Session 2 remained unfixed in later sessions
__pycache__/*.pyc binaries were committed into git in Sessions 1-5, adding persistent repo noise
Fixed relative path DATABASE='tasks.db' made the data layer non-configurable and test-unfriendly across all sessions
key_decisions: Session 2's JWT auth + users table with owner_id foreign key reframed the app from single-user CRUD to a multi-user system, and every later session built on that model
Session 3's introduction of Celery with a Redis broker/backend for async email notifications added an infrastructure dependency that Session 5's rate limiting also leaned on
Session 4's extraction of a BaseRepository ABC plus TaskRepository/UserRepository into repositories.py slimmed app.py and centralized all data access
Session 5's flask-limiter with Redis storage added a cross-cutting security concern reusing the already-present Redis dependency rather than introducing new infrastructure
Keeping all tests in a single test_app.py file (growing 12→38 tests) maintained a simple, always-green test surface
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and predictably across the five sessions. Session 1 established a minimal monolithic Flask+SQLite CRUD app; Session 2 added meaningful auth depth; Session 3 integrated an async Celery/Redis notification layer; Session 4 measurably reduced app.py complexity by extracting a repository layer; and Session 5 capped the arc with cross-cutting rate limiting and a near-doubling of test coverage to 38 tests. The codebase moved from a flat script toward layered structure (routes / repositories / celery config) with a consistently growing test suite, though security hygiene (hardcoded secret key) and per-request connection handling were never tightened.
story_review.summary: A logical, well-scoped greenfield-to-refined progression where each session layered naturally on the prior one and overall code quality improved across the arc, undermined only by security and connection-management debt that was never revisited.
